chunks.heading: Sarbanes–Oxley and SAP Security Controls
chunks.content: # Sarbanes–Oxley and SAP Security Controls

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.content:
## Overview

The Sarbanes–Oxley Act of 2002 is a United States statute. Section 404 requires management assessment of internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) and an accompanying auditor attestation for the issuers that the statute covers. Other SOX sections create different obligations, such as officer certification, and must not be collapsed into a single generic “SOX control.” SAP Security and GRC can support IT general controls and access evidence used in an ICFR program. Installing GRC does not make an organization SOX-compliant. Source checked 2026-10-21: 15 U.S.C. § 7262 (SOX Section 404), https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/7262; SAP Access Control and Process Control product documentation for the control and evidence mechanisms.

chunks.heading: Interview Summary
chunks.content: I would prepare SAP Security for a SOX ITGC audit by showing how joiner-mover-leaver, approvals, SoD, privileged access, access reviews, and change evidence operate for in-scope financial systems. I would not claim that GRC installation equals compliance.

chunks.heading: Prepare SAP Security for a SOX ITGC audit
chunks.section: Prepare SAP Security for a SOX ITGC audit
chunks.content: ## Prepare SAP Security for a SOX ITGC audit

chunks.heading: Prepare SAP Security for a SOX ITGC audit
chunks.section: Prepare SAP Security for a SOX ITGC audit
chunks.content: I would start from the in-scope financial processes and the ITGCs the auditors will test: access provisioning and deprovisioning, access approval, segregation of duties, privileged and emergency access, periodic user and role certification, and change management for roles and transports. For Access Control I would show the connector landscape, risk analysis results, mitigated versus open conflicts, access-request history, Firefighter logs with controller review, and completed access reviews. For role and authorization changes I would retain the transport evidence, profile generation and user comparison evidence where the ABAP system uses PFCG, and the business sign-off that the user can complete the intended financial task. Process Control can document and test the related controls when that product is in the control library, but a Process Control process is not the same object as a mitigation control.

chunks.heading: Prepare SAP Security for a SOX ITGC audit
chunks.section: Prepare SAP Security for a SOX ITGC audit
chunks.content: I would validate readiness with a sample population, evidence completeness, exception logs, and remediation ownership, and I would state that auditors test operating effectiveness over the period, not merely that a workflow exists. Source checked 2026-10-21: 15 U.S.C. § 7262; SAP Access Control and Process Control 12.0 documentation.

chunks.heading: Distinguish design effectiveness from operating effectiveness
chunks.section: Distinguish design effectiveness from operating effectiveness
chunks.content: I would separate control design from operating evidence. Design effectiveness asks whether the approved control would prevent or detect the risk if it operated as designed. Operating effectiveness asks whether the control actually operated over the audit period for a complete population or a justified sample. For SAP access, design may be the MSMP path, SoD ruleset, and Firefighter procedure. Operating evidence is the request history, risk analysis runs, mitigation reviews, FF log reviews, and certification completion for that period. A configured rule with no completed reviews is not operating evidence. Source checked 2026-10-21: ICFR practice framed against Section 404 management assessment obligations in 15 U.S.C. § 7262; SAP Access Control evidence artifacts.

chunks.heading: Role and Access Cutover
chunks.content: # Role and Access Cutover

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.content:
## Overview

Security cutover is the controlled move of users, roles, and identity jobs into production. Success is measured by expected access working, unexpected access absent, emergency access logged, and a rollback position the platform actually supports. SU53 is a defect diagnostic, not a cutover exit criterion. After users post business documents in the new or converted system, do not claim that a technical rollback is still available.

chunks.heading: Interview Summary
chunks.content:
Before go-live: freeze design, generate profiles, run PFUD/user comparison for existing assignments, reconcile AGR_USERS to the approved matrix, smoke-test critical business roles, confirm IPS/IAG/GRC jobs, and stage Firefighter IDs with owners and controllers.

At cutover: transport sequence, user status, birthright jobs, IdP/IAS trust, Cloud Connector if hybrid.

After: SUIM expected-vs-actual samples, UAT evidence from process owners, FF log review, IPS error queue, rollback transports or assignment restore if a wave fails.

chunks.heading: 30 Second Interview Answer
chunks.content: I would treat role cutover as a production event: approved matrix, generated roles, user comparison so existing users actually receive the new profile, smoke tests on critical processes, Firefighter ready with logging, and a rollback assignment list. I would not sign off cutover because one SU53 looked clean.

chunks.heading: 60 Second Interview Answer
chunks.content:
Validation pack: SUIM user-role and auth-object reports against the gold matrix; sample positive tests (can post) and negative tests (must fail); Fiori catalog/space visibility; IPS delta job for joiners created on cutover weekend; GRC/IAG request queue empty of blockers.

Emergency path: ID-based Firefighter via GRAC_SPM or IAG PAM, reason code tied to a ticket, controller review next business day. No unlogged SAP_ALL.

Rollback: keep the prior assignment extract; do not "fix" by widening a shared composite used by thousands of users.

chunks.heading: Go-Live Access Stabilization
chunks.content: # Go-Live Access Stabilization

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.content:
## Overview

Go-live for SAP security is the moment authentication, provisioning, and authorization must work together under real volume. The architect's job is a go/no-go on access risk, not a list of T-codes.

chunks.heading: Interview Summary
chunks.content:
Go/no-go checks: IdP/IAS trust valid, critical business roles smoke-tested, Firefighter available, batch and RFC users confirmed, IPS jobs green, SoD mitigations documented, rollback owner named.

First 72 hours: war-room triage by catalog vs org vs provisioning vs data; no casual role clones; daily FF review; defect-to-design feed for wave two.

chunks.heading: 30 Second Interview Answer
chunks.content: At go-live I would confirm that users can execute the processes we promised, that we can break-glass with an audit trail, and that we can reverse a bad wave. Stabilization is incident management plus catalog discipline, not widening roles because the phone is ringing.

chunks.heading: Related Topics
chunks.content:
Before go-live, freeze the approved access design, confirm IAS trust, smoke-test the critical business roles, confirm the IPS and IAG or GRC jobs, and name the rollback owner. At cutover, follow the rehearsed runbook: the transport or software-collection sequence, user status, and Cloud Connector when the landscape is hybrid. Hypercare is incident triage with a severity and an owner, not a second design phase. Close emergency access, review the Firefighter log daily, and leave hypercare when the open access backlog has an owner and a service level.

- knowledge/cutover/cutover-plan.md
- knowledge/hypercare/hypercare.md

chunks.heading: Security Cutover Rollback
chunks.content: # Security Cutover Rollback

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.content:
## Overview

A security rollback plan is the rehearsed way to restore a known-good access state when a cutover wave fails before the business has posted irreversibly in the new system. The plan is assignment extracts, transport sequencing, identity-job freezes, and go/no-go criteria. After users post business documents in a converted or newly live system, a full technical rollback may no longer be available. SU53 is not a rollback trigger and not cutover proof. Source checked 2026-10-21 against the repository cutover and hypercare procedures and SAP Activate cutover discipline already documented in knowledge/cutover/cutover-plan.md.

chunks.heading: Interview Summary
chunks.content: I would keep a rollback pack before go-live: prior AGR_USERS or business-role assignment extract, transport list, identity-job pause points, and Firefighter coverage. I would not promise a full platform reverse after productive posting.

chunks.heading: Prepare and execute a security rollback for a failed cutover wave
chunks.section: Prepare and execute a security rollback for a failed cutover wave
chunks.content: ## Prepare and execute a security rollback for a failed cutover wave

chunks.heading: Prepare and execute a security rollback for a failed cutover wave
chunks.section: Prepare and execute a security rollback for a failed cutover wave
chunks.content: I would prepare the rollback before the cutover window. I would freeze further role design, export the approved assignment baseline, list the transports that can be reversed or re-imported, confirm how user status and birthright jobs will be paused, and stage Firefighter IDs with owners and controllers for true blockers. During the wave I would use go/no-go checks on expected access working, unexpected access absent, and identity jobs completing without critical errors. If the wave fails before irreversible business posting, I would restore the prior assignment extract, reverse or withhold the failed transports according to the rehearsed sequence, re-run user comparison or the Public Edition business-role assignment restore for that deployment, and smoke-test critical processes with the restored access. After users have posted in the new or converted system, I would stop claiming a full technical rollback and move to defect containment, logged emergency access, and a forward fix.

chunks.heading: Prepare and execute a security rollback for a failed cutover wave
chunks.section: Prepare and execute a security rollback for a failed cutover wave
chunks.content: I would not widen a shared composite as a rollback shortcut, and I would not treat a clean SU53 as evidence that cutover or rollback succeeded.

chunks.heading: CyberArk Privileged Access Management (PAM) Architecture
chunks.content:
Spoken architect style: fluent Senior Principal Architect paragraphs — lead with exact T-codes/tables/utilities; never Decision/Mechanism/Governance/Validation headings.

**Product boundaries:** CyberArk Digital Vault, PVWA, CPM, PSM/PSMP, PTA, CCP/AAM, and related REST/PACLI administration. This is **not** SAP GRC EAM Firefighter alone and **not** a Vault installer guide—focus is HA/DR, Dual Control, rotation, session isolation, secrets for apps, detection, and audit evidence.

**Anti-surface rule:** Prefer `padr.ini`, Master Policy, `pm.log` / `PSMConsole.log` / `ITA.log`, CCP REST paths, and Dual Control mechanics over “what is CyberArk” definitions.

chunks.heading: Q1: How do you architect a High Availability (HA) and Disaster Recovery (DR) deployment for CyberArk Digital Vault across hybrid cloud environments?
chunks.section: Q1: How do you architect a High Availability (HA) and Disaster Recovery (DR) deployment for CyberArk Digital Vault across hybrid cloud environments?
chunks.content: ## Q1: How do you architect a High Availability (HA) and Disaster Recovery (DR) deployment for CyberArk Digital Vault across hybrid cloud environments?

chunks.heading: Q1: How do you architect a High Availability (HA) and Disaster Recovery (DR) deployment for CyberArk Digital Vault across hybrid cloud environments?
chunks.section: Q1: How do you architect a High Availability (HA) and Disaster Recovery (DR) deployment for CyberArk Digital Vault across hybrid cloud environments?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Deploy CyberArk Primary Vault with automatic failover to a Disaster Recovery (DR) Vault using asynchronous replication over Vault Protocol (TCP 1858), combined with load-balanced PVWA, CPM, and PSM component tiers.
- **Mechanism:** Configure `PADR` (PAM Disaster Recovery) service on the DR Vault node. Maintain `padr.ini` parameter `EnableFailover=YES` and `Interval=30` (seconds). In cloud deployments (AWS/Azure), utilize Vault Cluster / Distributed Vaults architecture. Configure PVWA `Vault.ini` pointing to Primary and DR Vault IPs with auto-switchover fallback.
- **Governance:** Mandate zero RPO for critical vault transactions by enforcing DB transaction log sync, and establish a sub-5-minute RTO policy for automated DR failover.
- **Validation:** Execute `PADR` status checks via `padr.log`; perform a controlled failover test by stopping PrivateArk Server service on Primary, and verify DR Vault transitions cleanly to Active mode (`FailoverHasStarted=1`).

chunks.heading: Q2: How do you design dual-control workflows and ticketing system integration (e.g., ServiceNow) inside CyberArk PVWA?
chunks.section: Q2: How do you design dual-control workflows and ticketing system integration (e.g., ServiceNow) inside CyberArk PVWA?
chunks.content: ## Q2: How do you design dual-control workflows and ticketing system integration (e.g., ServiceNow) inside CyberArk PVWA?

chunks.heading: Q2: How do you design dual-control workflows and ticketing system integration (e.g., ServiceNow) inside CyberArk PVWA?
chunks.section: Q2: How do you design dual-control workflows and ticketing system integration (e.g., ServiceNow) inside CyberArk PVWA?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Enforce Dual Control and mandatory Ticket System Validation at the Safe/Master Policy layer to require dual authorization and active change ticket verification before credentials can be checked out or brokered.
- **Mechanism:** In PVWA Master Policy, enable *Require dual control password access approval* and *Require ticket system integration*. Configure ServiceNow Ticketing parameters under PVWA Administration → Options → Ticketing Systems. Specify REST API connection settings (`TicketURL`, `ServiceNowAuth`) to validate ticket state (`State = In Progress`) via API calls before releasing credentials.
- **Governance:** Prohibit Emergency/Break-Glass accounts from ticketing dependencies by isolating them in dedicated Safes with explicit EAM/PAM approval paths.
- **Validation:** Attempt credential checkout via PVWA entering a closed/fake ServiceNow Incident ID; verify system displays ticket validation failure and blocks password checkout.

chunks.heading: Q3: How do you configure Central Policy Manager (CPM) for automatic password rotation and reconciliation across Windows, Unix, and Database targets?
chunks.section: Q3: How do you configure Central Policy Manager (CPM) for automatic password rotation and reconciliation across Windows, Unix, and Database targets?
chunks.content: ## Q3: How do you configure Central Policy Manager (CPM) for automatic password rotation and reconciliation across Windows, Unix, and Database targets?

chunks.heading: Q3: How do you configure Central Policy Manager (CPM) for automatic password rotation and reconciliation across Windows, Unix, and Database targets?
chunks.section: Q3: How do you configure Central Policy Manager (CPM) for automatic password rotation and reconciliation across Windows, Unix, and Database targets?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Utilize CPM policy platforms to enforce periodic automatic credential rotation, post-usage immediate changes, and reconciliation via dedicated privileged reconcile accounts.
- **Mechanism:** Configure Master Policy settings: `Perform periodic change = Yes` and `MinValidityPeriod = 1 day`. In platform settings, define `ChangePasswordInResetMode = Yes`. Specify Reconcile Account association at the Safe or Account level. CPM uses `pm.log` and `CPMScanner` to trigger target password changes via SSH, WMI/WinRM, or SQL connection plugins.
- **Governance:** Require daily reconciliation checks and enforce CPM automatic account lockouts if password rotation fails more than 3 consecutive times.
- **Validation:** Force a CPM password change in PVWA; verify status transitions from `Pending Change` to `Success` and check `pm.log` on the CPM server to validate execution.

chunks.heading: Q4: How do you broker zero-trust privileged sessions using Privileged Session Manager (PSM) and PSM for SSH (PSMP) without exposing credentials to end users?
chunks.section: Q4: How do you broker zero-trust privileged sessions using Privileged Session Manager (PSM) and PSM for SSH (PSMP) without exposing credentials to end users?
chunks.content: ## Q4: How do you broker zero-trust privileged sessions using Privileged Session Manager (PSM) and PSM for SSH (PSMP) without exposing credentials to end users?

chunks.heading: Q4: How do you broker zero-trust privileged sessions using Privileged Session Manager (PSM) and PSM for SSH (PSMP) without exposing credentials to end users?
chunks.section: Q4: How do you broker zero-trust privileged sessions using Privileged Session Manager (PSM) and PSM for SSH (PSMP) without exposing credentials to end users?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Route all administrative access through PSM/PSMP isolation proxies, enforcing complete credential masking, live session monitoring, and video/keystroke recording.
- **Mechanism:** Users connect via PVWA or native client (RDP/SSH) targeting PSM proxy endpoint. PSM retrieves target credentials securely from Digital Vault via Vault protocol (TCP 1858) and initiates RDP/SSH session to target using native protocols (TCP 3389 / 22). Enable PSM HTML5 Gateway for clientless web-browser RDP/SSH access. Configure PSM Hardened server with AppLocker rules restricting execution strictly to authorized binaries (`mstsc.exe`, `putty.exe`).
- **Governance:** Enforce full video session recording and text transcript logging for all tier-0 administrative sessions.
- **Validation:** Launch a PSM RDP session, attempt to copy/paste text or launch unapproved executables, and verify AppLocker blocks execution while `PSMConsole.log` logs the policy violation.

chunks.heading: Q5: How do you secure DevOps pipelines and microservices using CyberArk Application Access Manager (AAM) / Central Credential Provider (CCP)?
chunks.section: Q5: How do you secure DevOps pipelines and microservices using CyberArk Application Access Manager (AAM) / Central Credential Provider (CCP)?
chunks.content: ## Q5: How do you secure DevOps pipelines and microservices using CyberArk Application Access Manager (AAM) / Central Credential Provider (CCP)?

chunks.heading: Q5: How do you secure DevOps pipelines and microservices using CyberArk Application Access Manager (AAM) / Central Credential Provider (CCP)?
chunks.section: Q5: How do you secure DevOps pipelines and microservices using CyberArk Application Access Manager (AAM) / Central Credential Provider (CCP)?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Deploy Central Credential Provider (CCP) agentless REST API architecture or Application Access Manager (AAM) local dynamic caching to eliminate hardcoded secrets in CI/CD pipelines and microservices.
- **Mechanism:** Applications issue HTTPS REST calls to CCP endpoint (`/AIMWebService/api/Accounts`). Authenticate application identity using mTLS client certificates, IP whitelisting, and OS User validation defined in CyberArk Application ID settings. CCP fetches requested secret from Digital Vault in real time and returns JSON payload without storing secrets on app servers.
- **Governance:** Prohibit static API keys or long-lived tokens in source code repositories (Git); mandate mTLS certificate-based app authentication.
- **Validation:** Issue a curl/REST request presenting a valid client certificate to the CCP endpoint and verify JSON secret retrieval payload with `HTTP 200 OK`.

chunks.heading: Q6: How do you design Privileged Threat Analytics (PTA) detection use cases for Vault, domain, and session abuse?
chunks.section: Q6: How do you design Privileged Threat Analytics (PTA) detection use cases for Vault, domain, and session abuse?
chunks.content: ## Q6: How do you design Privileged Threat Analytics (PTA) detection use cases for Vault, domain, and session abuse?

chunks.heading: Q6: How do you design Privileged Threat Analytics (PTA) detection use cases for Vault, domain, and session abuse?
chunks.section: Q6: How do you design Privileged Threat Analytics (PTA) detection use cases for Vault, domain, and session abuse?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Position PTA as the detection plane for privileged anomalies (credential theft patterns, suspicious Vault activity, risky PSM behavior)—not as a replacement for CPM rotation or PSM isolation.
- **Mechanism:** Deploy PTA to ingest Vault syslog/audit and relevant Windows/AD security events where licensed. Enable detections for patterns such as anomalous Retrieve/Connect sequences, Pass-the-Hash / Golden Ticket indicators (environment-dependent), and abnormal privileged account usage. Forward PTA alerts to SOC SIEM (Sentinel/Splunk) with Account, Safe, User, and SourceIP context. Correlate PTA alert IDs with Vault audit (`ITALog` / Vault audit exports) and PSM recordings.
- **Governance:** High/Critical PTA alerts follow 24/7 SOC playbooks; false-positive tuning requires Security + IAM dual approval.
- **Validation:** Reproduce a controlled anomalous Retrieve/Connect in non-Production; confirm PTA raises an alert, SIEM ticket opens, and Vault/`ITALog` entries match the PTA event timeline.

chunks.heading: Q7: How do you administer CyberArk at scale using REST APIs and PACLI without weakening Dual Control?
chunks.section: Q7: How do you administer CyberArk at scale using REST APIs and PACLI without weakening Dual Control?
chunks.content: ## Q7: How do you administer CyberArk at scale using REST APIs and PACLI without weakening Dual Control?

chunks.heading: Q7: How do you administer CyberArk at scale using REST APIs and PACLI without weakening Dual Control?
chunks.section: Q7: How do you administer CyberArk at scale using REST APIs and PACLI without weakening Dual Control?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Automate Safe/Account lifecycle via CyberArk REST (PVWA API) and constrain PACLI/CLI to break-glass automation identities—never bypass Dual Control for Production Retrieve.
- **Mechanism:**
 - REST: authenticate to PVWA API (`/PasswordVault/API/Auth/...`), then manage Safes/Accounts/Platforms via documented endpoints (e.g. Accounts, Safes, Members).
 - Automation identities: dedicated AppID/user with least Safe permissions (`Add accounts`, `Update account properties`)—exclude unconstrained `Retrieve` on tier-0 Safes.
 - PACLI: reserved for emergency Vault operations with logged operator ID; store scripts in controlled repo; no embedded Vault admin passwords (CCP for script secrets).
- **Governance:** All Production API clients registered; client credentials rotated; Dual Control remains enforced for human Retrieve/Connect.

chunks.heading: Q7: How do you administer CyberArk at scale using REST APIs and PACLI without weakening Dual Control?
chunks.section: Q7: How do you administer CyberArk at scale using REST APIs and PACLI without weakening Dual Control?
chunks.content: - **Validation:** API create/update Account succeeds; API Retrieve on Dual Control Safe without confirmation fails; Vault audit shows API user actions separately from human PVWA sessions.

chunks.heading: Q8: How do you segment Safes and Master Policy for tier-0 (domain/cloud admin) versus application technical accounts?
chunks.section: Q8: How do you segment Safes and Master Policy for tier-0 (domain/cloud admin) versus application technical accounts?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Separate Safes and policy overlays by risk tier so tier-0 secrets never share membership or recording policy with routine app accounts.
- **Mechanism:**
 - Safes: `T0-DOMAIN`, `T0-CLOUD-HYPERVISOR`, `APP-<PLATFORM>-TECH` naming.
 - Master Policy defaults: Dual Control + PSM required for T0; CPM periodic change for all; exclusive accounts for shared break-glass where needed.
 - Platform bindings: Windows Domain Admin vs SQL vs Network Device platforms with distinct reconcile accounts.
 - Membership: T0 confirmer group ≠ T0 requestor group; auditors get view/recording without Connect.
- **Governance:** Architecture Board must approve any Safe that mixes T0 and app credentials; quarterly membership SoD report.
- **Validation:** User in APP Safe cannot list T0 accounts; T0 Connect requires Dual Control + recording; export Safe member report shows SoD separation.

chunks.heading: Q9: How do you integrate CyberArk with SAP hybrid landscapes so technical users are vaulted while human Firefighter stays in SAP IAG/GRC EAM?
chunks.section: Q9: How do you integrate CyberArk with SAP hybrid landscapes so technical users are vaulted while human Firefighter stays in SAP IAG/GRC EAM?
chunks.content: ## Q9: How do you integrate CyberArk with SAP hybrid landscapes so technical users are vaulted while human Firefighter stays in SAP IAG/GRC EAM?

chunks.heading: Q9: How do you integrate CyberArk with SAP hybrid landscapes so technical users are vaulted while human Firefighter stays in SAP IAG/GRC EAM?
chunks.section: Q9: How do you integrate CyberArk with SAP hybrid landscapes so technical users are vaulted while human Firefighter stays in SAP IAG/GRC EAM?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Split control planes—**CyberArk** vaults and rotates machine/technical credentials (RFC, OS, DB, BTP Destination secrets); **SAP IAG PAM / GRC EAM** handles human emergency elevation with SAP audit logs.
- **Mechanism:** Onboard SAP System/Communication users into CPM platforms; consumers (`SM59`, BTP Destinations, middleware) retrieve via CCP or controlled secret sync after rotation. Human Firefighter / Role Collection elevation remains in IAG/EAM with `GRAC_SPM_LOG_SYNC` / BTP audit review. Document RACI: IAM owns Vault; SAP Security owns EAM/IAG; Platform owns Destination updates post-CPM change.
- **Governance:** Reject designs that put interactive Firefighter passwords only in CyberArk without SAP session audit—or leave interface passwords in clear text outside Vault.
- **Validation:** Tabletop: interface outage remediated via CPM/CCP evidence (`pm.log`, CCP `HTTP 200`); human emergency remediated via IAM/EAM evidence—both ticket types close with the correct tool artifacts.

chunks.heading: Q10: What Production go-live and audit evidence pack do you require for CyberArk PAM?
chunks.section: Q10: What Production go-live and audit evidence pack do you require for CyberArk PAM?
chunks.content: ## Q10: What Production go-live and audit evidence pack do you require for CyberArk PAM?

chunks.heading: Q10: What Production go-live and audit evidence pack do you require for CyberArk PAM?
chunks.section: Q10: What Production go-live and audit evidence pack do you require for CyberArk PAM?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Accept Production only on policy, SoD, rotation, session, DR, and SIEM evidence—component “installed” is not acceptance.
- **Mechanism:** Evidence checklist:
 1. Master Policy export (Dual Control, ticketing, PSM required, change intervals).
 2. Safe inventory + requestor/confirmer SoD report.
 3. Sample CPM Change/Verify successes from `pm.log`.
 4. PSM recording sample + AppLocker deny from `PSMConsole.log`.
 5. CCP mTLS retrieve proof (`HTTP 200`) for one app identity.
 6. Controlled `PADR` failover evidence (`padr.log`, `FailoverHasStarted=1`).
 7. PTA/SIEM alert test ticket.
 8. Break-glass Safe procedure + last drill record.
- **Governance:** CISO / Internal Audit sign-off; quarterly drift review against the pack.
- **Validation:** Auditor selects a random Production Account; team produces Dual Control → Connect/Change artifacts and recording without exposing clear-text secrets on the auditor workstation.

chunks.heading: SAP Datasphere Access
chunks.content: # SAP Datasphere Access

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.content:
## Overview

Datasphere authorization is space-centric. It is not SAC folder security and not S/4 PFCG. Interviews test whether you keep those models separate even when a story in SAC is fed by a live Datasphere connection.

chunks.heading: Interview Summary
chunks.content: Users are assigned to spaces with scoped privileges on views, tables, and data access controls. Row-level restrictions belong in Datasphere data access controls or source-system authorizations, depending on how the view is built. SAC then adds its own team and story permissions on top. SSO through IAS does not imply space access.

chunks.heading: 30 Second Interview Answer
chunks.content: I would design Datasphere security around spaces: who is a member, what they can consume or deploy, and which data access controls restrict rows. I would not reuse an S/4 role catalog as the Datasphere model. If SAC is in front, I would treat SAC content permission and Datasphere space permission as two checks that both have to pass.

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.content:
## Procedure

1. The user can already sign in through the identity provider trusted by the tenant. Sign-in does not grant a space.
2. Add the user to the space with a scoped role such as modeler or viewer. Do not use a tenant-wide administrator role to grant one space.
3. Restrict rows with a data access control on the view, or with the source system's authorizations when the view only consumes that source.
4. If a SAC story reads the space, the user still needs the SAC team and the story permission. Space membership does not open the story.

chunks.heading: Distinctions
chunks.content:
## Distinctions

- SAC: teams, folders, stories
- Datasphere: spaces, privileges, data access controls
- HANA Cloud underneath: database privileges if consumed directly
- IAS: who logged in

chunks.heading: Fiori Catalogs and Target Mappings
chunks.content: # Fiori Catalogs and Target Mappings

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.content:
## Overview

A Fiori catalog holds the tiles and target mappings that make an app resolvable on the launchpad. Catalog assignment alone does not prove the user can complete the business task. Runtime authorization still depends on the deployment. Source checked 2026-10-21 against knowledge/fiori/fiori-security.md and the SAP Learning / KBA sources recorded there.

chunks.heading: Interview Summary
chunks.content: I would treat a missing app as a catalog, space, page, or role-assignment problem before any authorization trace.

chunks.heading: Check catalog and target mapping for a missing Fiori app
chunks.section: Check catalog and target mapping for a missing Fiori app
chunks.content: I would confirm the deployment first. On SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition I would use Maintain Business Users and Maintain Business Roles and verify the business catalog and IAM app assignment. Public Edition does not use PFCG or /UI2/FLPCM_CUST for that check. On Private Edition or on-premise I would confirm that the PFCG role contains the catalog and that the catalog contains the tile and target mapping, using /UI2/FLPCM_CUST or /UI2/FLPCM_CONF according to the client versus configuration layer. I would not start SU53 for a missing app. I would validate by searching the launchpad as the affected user and confirming the app appears for the intended business task.

chunks.heading: Sources and scope
chunks.content:
- knowledge/fiori/fiori-security.md
- SAP Learning, Managing Content on the SAP Fiori Launchpad; KBA 3499342 for Public Edition missing-app checks

chunks.heading: SAP Fiori & Front-End Security Architecture
chunks.content:
Spoken architect style: fluent Senior Principal Architect paragraphs — lead with exact T-codes/tables/utilities; never Decision/Mechanism/Governance/Validation headings.

**Product boundaries:** Fiori launchpad visibility (catalogs / spaces / pages) is **not** the same as backend execution authorization. Front-end roles grant tiles and target mappings; backend PFCG (or Public Edition business roles) enforce OData/S_SERVICE and business object checks. Gateway (`/IWFND/*`) and backend are often separate systems in hub deployments.

**Anti-surface rule:** Prefer space/page content, OData service activation, `STAUTHTRACE` on backend, and missing-tile vs 403 diagnosis over “assign the Fiori role.”

chunks.heading: Q1: How do you design front-end versus backend roles so tiles appear only when the user can execute?
chunks.section: Q1: How do you design front-end versus backend roles so tiles appear only when the user can execute?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Pair every launchpad content assignment with backend authorizations for the same apps—never ship a “tile-only” composite in Production.
- **Mechanism:** Front-end: business catalogs + spaces/pages (or groups/catalogs on older releases) in a Fiori PFCG role. Backend: OData service authorizations (`S_SERVICE` / start authorizations) and application objects from SU24 proposals. In embedded deployments one role may hold both; in hub, transport FE and BE roles as a set and assign both.
- **Governance:** Definition of Done for an app role includes FE content + BE auth + negative test. Orphan FE catalogs without BE are audit defects.
- **Validation:** User sees tile; app loads; `STAUTHTRACE` RC=0; remove BE auth → tile may show but app fails with auth error—treat as failed design and fix pairing.

chunks.heading: Q2: How do you use spaces and pages without creating uncontrolled personalization shadow access?
chunks.section: Q2: How do you use spaces and pages without creating uncontrolled personalization shadow access?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Spaces/pages are the governed navigation structure; personalization must not become a path to unauthorized apps.
- **Mechanism:** Maintain spaces/pages via Fiori Launchpad App Manager / Manage Launchpad Spaces (release-dependent). Assign space to role. Restrict who can create public content. Avoid assigning broad catalogs “SAP_*” wholesale to business users.
- **Governance:** Content owners approve space changes; Security reviews addition of admin/diagnostic apps to business spaces.
- **Validation:** User role shows only intended pages; app not in space is unreachable via search if catalog not assigned; transport of space content RC=0.

chunks.heading: Q3: How do you troubleshoot missing tile versus application launch failure?
chunks.section: Q3: How do you troubleshoot missing tile versus application launch failure?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Missing tile = content/assignment problem; tile present but error = service/backend auth or configuration problem—do not conflate.
- **Mechanism:** Missing tile: check role catalogs, space/page assignment, cache (`/UI2/INVALIDATE_*` where applicable), user comparison. Launch failure: `/IWFND/ERROR_LOG`, `/IWBEP/ERROR_LOG`, `STAUTHTRACE` on backend user, ICF node active (`SICF`), service activated (`/IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE`). Confirm system alias and RFC to backend in hub.
- **Governance:** Production cache indiscriminate clears scheduled; auth fixes via transport. Temporary `SAP_ALL` banned.
- **Validation:** Catalog assign → tile appears; BE object add → app runs; error log empty on success path.

chunks.heading: Q4: How do you authorize OData and ICF dependencies for custom and standard Fiori apps?
chunks.section: Q4: How do you authorize OData and ICF dependencies for custom and standard Fiori apps?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Every app’s OData services are allowlisted and proposed in SU24—custom services get the same discipline as standard.
- **Mechanism:** Identify services from app documentation / `/IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE`; maintain SU24 proposals; activate ICF nodes needed; assign in backend role. For draft/UI5 freestyle apps, include additional RFC/function auth if used. CDS service bindings follow the release’s auth model (`S_SERVICE`, DCL where applicable).
- **Governance:** Unregistered custom OData in Production is a security finding. Service activation changes require change control.
- **Validation:** `STAUTHTRACE` shows service check pass; deactivate service → controlled failure; custom app UAT with least-privilege role.

chunks.heading: Q5: How do you integrate Fiori SSO (IAS / SAML / OIDC) without weakening backend authorization?
chunks.section: Q5: How do you integrate Fiori SSO (IAS / SAML / OIDC) without weakening backend authorization?
chunks.content: **Aliases / interview phrasing:** configure Fiori SSO; Fiori SSO setup; IAS Fiori setup; SAML2 Fiori Launchpad; Principal Propagation; OIDC FLP trust.

chunks.heading: Q5: How do you integrate Fiori SSO (IAS / SAML / OIDC) without weakening backend authorization?
chunks.section: Q5: How do you integrate Fiori SSO (IAS / SAML / OIDC) without weakening backend authorization?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** SSO establishes identity to FLP; backend still enforces ABAP authorizations for the mapped user—trusted RFC must not become universal trust.
- **Mechanism:** Configure FLP authentication (SAML/OIDC via IAS); ensure principal propagation / user mapping to backend. Harden `SM59` trusted connections; avoid hard-coded technical users for interactive apps. For Principal Propagation scenarios, validate CERTRULE / short-lived X.509 patterns where used with Cloud Connector.
- **Governance:** Technical user fallback for interactive Fiori is prohibited. IdP group ≠ backend role unless explicitly provisioned.
- **Validation:** SSO user without BE role denied on app data calls; propagation test shows correct backend `SY-UNAME`; trusted RFC misconfig caught in negative test.

chunks.heading: Q6: How do you secure Fiori apps used for GRC and other privileged admin tools?
chunks.section: Q6: How do you secure Fiori apps used for GRC and other privileged admin tools?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** GRC/IAG/admin Fiori apps are privileged—assigned via admin composites or Firefighter, not business employee launches.
- **Mechanism:** Isolate GRC NWBC/Fiori catalogs into security-admin roles; require GRC/IAG entitlements behind them. Do not place Access Request admin apps in employee spaces.
- **Governance:** Quarterly review of who has GRC Fiori admin catalogs. Break-glass for emergency access management UI.
- **Validation:** Business user search cannot launch GRC config apps; admin user can; SUIM shows catalog restricted.

chunks.heading: Q7: How do you validate Fiori security during S/4HANA conversion or Fiori upgrade?
chunks.section: Q7: How do you validate Fiori security during S/4HANA conversion or Fiori upgrade?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Treat content delta (deprecated apps, successor apps, new services) as a security work item in Realize—not a Basis-only upgrade task.
- **Mechanism:** Run app obsolescence analysis; remap catalogs to successor apps; SU25/SU24 for new checks; regression test persona scripts; invalidate caches post-import. Update spaces/pages to remove dead tiles.
- **Governance:** Go-live blocked if critical process apps lack FE+BE pairing after upgrade. Defects tracked with app IDs.
- **Validation:** Persona UAT on successor apps; `STAUTHTRACE` clean; no critical missing tiles in Production smoke.

chunks.heading: Q8: How do you handle key-user extensibility and custom tiles safely?
chunks.section: Q8: How do you handle key-user extensibility and custom tiles safely?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Key-user and custom UI adaptations are extensions—authorize who can adapt, and ensure underlying services remain least privilege.
- **Mechanism:** Restrict adaptation authorizations; transport adaptations where required; ensure custom tile target mappings point to approved services. Review custom CDS DCLs for data exposure.
- **Governance:** Clean-core preference: prefer in-app extensibility with security review over uncontrolled IDE deploys. Production direct adapt limited.
- **Validation:** Key user without adapt auth cannot change UI; custom tile denied without service auth; DCL deny evidenced for restricted company code.

chunks.heading: Q9: How do you performance- and security-test catalog assignment at scale?
chunks.section: Q9: How do you performance- and security-test catalog assignment at scale?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Avoid mega-catalogs that dump thousands of apps into a role—performance and audit both suffer.
- **Mechanism:** Build persona-sized catalogs; use spaces to structure; monitor FLP load; periodically remove unused apps via usage analytics where available. Composite assignment still requires user comparison.
- **Governance:** Catalog size standards in naming/design guidelines. Security rejects “assign all SAP business catalogs.”
- **Validation:** FLP loads within accepted SLA; SUIM shows intentional catalog set; unused admin apps absent from business roles.

chunks.heading: Q10: What evidence proves Fiori access control for audit or Deploy gate?
chunks.section: Q10: What evidence proves Fiori access control for audit or Deploy gate?
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Evidence = role→space/catalog matrix, backend object pairing, SSO config summary, and positive/negative test results per critical app.
- **Mechanism:** Export role menus/catalogs; list OData services; attach traces; document hub vs embedded; include cache-refresh procedure in runbook.
- **Governance:** Deploy quality gate requires security sign-off on critical persona apps.
- **Validation:** Walkthrough: missing BE auth fails app; missing catalog hides tile; SSO user mapping correct; transport list matches QAS tested content.

chunks.heading: Fiori Launchpad and App Authorization
chunks.content: # Fiori Launchpad and App Authorization

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.content:
## Overview

Fiori authorization is a front-end visibility model plus a backend execution model. Which tool applies depends on the deployment. On SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, a missing app starts in Maintain Business Users and Maintain Business Roles: the assigned business role, the business catalog, the IAM Apps active flag, and the assigned launchpad space. SAP Knowledge Base Article 3499342 documents that path. Launchpad Designer, PFCG, and an ABAP trace are not the Public Edition procedure. On Private Edition and on-premise, the PFCG role must contain the catalog and the space, and the catalog must contain the tile and the target mapping. /UI2/FLPCM_CUST is client-specific and /UI2/FLPCM_CONF is cross-client.

chunks.heading: Design Fiori security for an S/4 rollout
chunks.section: Design Fiori security for an S/4 rollout
chunks.content: ## Design Fiori security for an S/4 rollout

chunks.heading: Design Fiori security for an S/4 rollout
chunks.section: Design Fiori security for an S/4 rollout
chunks.content: Design Fiori security as launchpad visibility plus runtime authorization, and keep the administration path with the deployment. Use Maintain Business Roles to assign business catalogs, spaces, and pages on SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, then assign that business role in Maintain Business Users. Public Edition does not use PFCG, SU53, or /UI2/FLPCM_CUST. Maintain the catalog and target mapping in /UI2/FLPCM_CUST or /UI2/FLPCM_CONF on Private Edition and on-premise, and assign the catalog and space in the PFCG role. A missing app is a catalog, space, page, or role-assignment problem. An app that opens and then fails is a runtime authorization problem. Inspect Display Authorization Trace on Public Edition only after the app opens and a check fails. Use transaction SU53 on an ABAP system only to read the last failed authorization check, and do not treat that display as proof that access succeeded. Validate the design by having the assigned user complete the intended business task in the app.

chunks.heading: Interview Summary
chunks.content: A business role in S/4HANA is not just a composite of single roles. It must include the catalog or space assignment that exposes apps and the runtime authorization required by the app's services and business logic. The implementation differs between Public Edition and customer-managed ABAP systems; designing only PFCG menus does not cover the launchpad and service layers.

chunks.heading: 30 Second Interview Answer
chunks.content: I would split Fiori security into launchpad visibility and runtime authorization. In Public Edition, business roles, catalogs, spaces, and pages control app availability; in customer-managed ABAP deployments, the corresponding launchpad content and PFCG role apply. Runtime service checks depend on OData version: V2 may use IWSG/IWSV and S_SERVICE defaults; V4 uses G4BA with S_START. CDS DCL and application checks protect business data and actions. I would first identify the failing layer and then use evidence from that layer.

chunks.heading: 60 Second Interview Answer
chunks.content:
The launchpad content model depends on edition and release. Public Edition uses business roles with catalogs and spaces/pages. Customer-managed ABAP systems may use groups on older releases or spaces/pages on newer releases; catalog and space assignments are made through the launchpad content tools and PFCG. Confirm the target release instead of saying groups disappeared everywhere.

For an app that opens but fails, identify its OData version and deployment before adding service authorizations: V2 and V4 use different service authorization models, and application-specific checks still apply. Copying a GUI role and expecting the Fiori service and data checks to work is a common conversion defect.

Troubleshooting uses the launchpad content manager and backend traces differently. /IWFND/ERROR_LOG and STAUTHTRACE tell you about failed service calls. They will not explain a missing space assignment.

chunks.heading: 60 Second Interview Answer
chunks.content: Trade-off: one fat catalog is easy to assign and terrible to certify. Fine-grained catalogs map better to job functions and SoD but explode maintenance. I would align catalogs to process areas and let business roles assemble them, not the other way around.

chunks.heading: Architecture
chunks.content:
## Architecture

- Business catalog: tiles and target mappings
- Space and page: user-facing navigation
- PFCG role: catalog assignment plus OData plus objects
- OData runtime: applicable V2 IWSG/IWSV and S_SERVICE, or V4 G4BA and S_START, plus application checks
- SU24: authorization defaults for applicable ABAP services and transactions; not a universal cloud or V4 configuration step

chunks.heading: Common Defects
chunks.content:
- Tile visible, 403 or no data — backend or DCL/CDS access
- No tile — catalog or space not on the user
- App works in GUI, fails in Fiori — service missing from role
- Custom app with no SU24 — empty proposals, manual objects, drift at upgrade

chunks.heading: Deployment model
chunks.content:
Verified 2026-10-13. Do not use one transaction for every S/4HANA deployment.

On SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition and on-premise, launchpad content has two layers. Transaction /UI2/FLPCM_CONF is the cross-client configuration layer. Transaction /UI2/FLPCM_CUST is the client-specific customizing layer, and client-specific changes supersede configuration. Spaces and pages are maintained in the Manage Launchpad Spaces and Manage Launchpad Pages apps, then assigned to a PFCG role. Spaces and pages do not grant authorization. A tile the user is not authorized to start is hidden. Groups can still exist on older on-premise releases. Spaces and pages are the recommended layout in newer on-premise releases, not a universal replacement that deletes groups. Source: SAP Learning, Managing Content on the SAP Fiori Launchpad, Implementing SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition; SAP Learning, Creating SAP Fiori Spaces and Pages.

chunks.heading: Deployment model
chunks.content: On SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, customers do not use /UI2/FLPCM_CUST, PFCG, or Launchpad Designer. Spaces and pages are assigned from the business role in Maintain Business Roles, using Manage Launchpad Spaces and Manage Launchpad Pages. If the catalog is assigned and the app is still missing, KBA 3499342 says to check the IAM Apps tab and whether the application category is a direct application or only a navigation target. SAP Note 3401525 describes the spaces migration and the Manage Launchpad Settings parameters SPACES and SPACES_ENABLE_USER. The note text available here does not say that every new tenant has group mode removed. Confirm the parameter on the tenant. Source checked 2026-10-13: SAP Learning, Managing Spaces and Pages; KBA 3499342; SAP Note 3401525 title and public FAQ text.

chunks.heading: Deployment model
chunks.content: If the tile is missing, stay on launchpad resolution for that deployment. Public Edition: Maintain Business Users, Maintain Business Roles, and Manage Launchpad Spaces. Private Edition or on-premise: the PFCG role, the catalog, the target mapping, and /UI2/FLPCM_CUST or /UI2/FLPCM_CONF. Do not start a missing tile in STAUTHTRACE or SU53. If the tile opens and a request fails on an ABAP Gateway system, read /IWFND/ERROR_LOG on the hub and /IWBEP/ERROR_LOG on the backend, and use the HTTP status and error text before any authorization trace. Use /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE only for registration and activation. On Public Edition, the opened-app check is Display Authorization Trace, not those transactions.

chunks.heading: Troubleshoot a user who cannot access a Fiori app
chunks.section: Troubleshoot a user who cannot access a Fiori app
chunks.content: ## Troubleshoot a user who cannot access a Fiori app

chunks.heading: Troubleshoot a user who cannot access a Fiori app
chunks.section: Troubleshoot a user who cannot access a Fiori app
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** Separate a missing app (launchpad content / role assignment) from an opened app that fails at runtime, and select tools only after confirming Public Edition versus on-premise / Private Edition.
- **Mechanism:** Public Edition: Maintain Business Users, Maintain Business Roles, then Display Authorization Trace only after the app opens and an authorization check fails. Public Edition does not use PFCG, SU53, or Gateway error logs for that check. On-premise or Private Edition: confirm the user's PFCG role contains the catalog and target mapping before runtime service diagnosis; if the app is visible but fails, inspect browser errors and Gateway logs in /IWFND/ERROR_LOG and /IWBEP/ERROR_LOG for that topology.
- **Governance:** Do not treat a Public Edition business role as interchangeable with an on-premise PFCG role; keep edition-correct tooling.

chunks.heading: Troubleshoot a user who cannot access a Fiori app
chunks.section: Troubleshoot a user who cannot access a Fiori app
chunks.content: - **Validation:** Use SU53 or STAUTHTRACE only when the log shows an authorization failure — SU53 displays the last failed authorization check and is not proof that access succeeded. Correct the demonstrated cause, then have the affected user complete the intended business task in the app.

chunks.heading: Troubleshoot Fiori access when the server is on premise
chunks.section: Troubleshoot Fiori access when the server is on premise
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** On-premise ABAP Fiori troubleshooting starts with launchpad content and PFCG assignment, not with an authorization trace for a missing app.
- **Mechanism:** Check the user's PFCG role and whether that role contains the catalog and the target mapping for the app. If the app opens and still errors, reproduce and inspect the browser error plus Gateway logs in /IWFND/ERROR_LOG and /IWBEP/ERROR_LOG for the actual frontend/backend topology; do not assume every system uses a hub.
- **Governance:** Keep missing-app diagnosis on content/role assignment; do not jump to SU53 for a tile that never launches.
- **Validation:** Use SU53 or STAUTHTRACE only when the log shows an authorization failure — SU53 shows the last failed check rather than proof of success. Correct the demonstrated cause and have the affected user complete the intended business task.

chunks.heading: Fiori app missing from the launchpad
chunks.section: Fiori app missing from the launchpad
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** A missing app is a launchpad content or role-assignment problem; do not start with a runtime authorization display.
- **Mechanism:** Public Edition: Maintain Business Users and Maintain Business Roles; confirm catalog, space, and page. On-premise: check the PFCG role, the catalog, and the target mapping.
- **Governance:** Do not use SU53 to explain a missing app — that display is the last failed authorization check after a request has already run.
- **Validation:** Search the launchpad as the affected user and confirm the app is available for the intended business task.

chunks.heading: Fiori app opens and returns an authorization error
chunks.section: Fiori app opens and returns an authorization error
chunks.content:
- **Decision:** When the app opens and then fails authorization, reproduce first and read the error text before changing a role.
- **Mechanism:** Public Edition: Display Authorization Trace; correct only the failed authorization or restriction evidence. On-premise: inspect /IWFND/ERROR_LOG and /IWBEP/ERROR_LOG, then use SU53 or STAUTHTRACE only if the log shows an authorization failure.
- **Governance:** Do not widen roles beyond the demonstrated failure object or restriction.
- **Validation:** Have the user complete the intended business task after the fix. SU53 is not proof that the task succeeded.

chunks.heading: Public Edition troubleshooting: app is missing
chunks.section: Public Edition troubleshooting: app is missing
chunks.content: ## Public Edition troubleshooting: app is missing

chunks.heading: Public Edition troubleshooting: app is missing
chunks.section: Public Edition troubleshooting: app is missing
chunks.content: First ask the user to search App Finder or All My Apps in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2608. SAP Help says App Finder lists apps available for the user's role, while a launchpad page shows only the subset selected by the administrator. If the app is in App Finder but absent from the expected page, inspect the role's space assignment and page content in Manage Launchpad Spaces and Manage Launchpad Pages. If it is absent from App Finder, use Maintain Business Users to confirm the user's assigned business roles, then Maintain Business Roles and IAM Information System to verify the business catalog or direct IAM app assignment and activation. Check restrictions or scope only if they explain the app's eligibility. KBA 3499342 also covers a navigation-target application with no tile. These are Fiori apps, not transactions. A missing app is not an OData authorization trace case; use Display Authorization Trace only after the app opens and a runtime authorization check fails.

chunks.heading: Public Edition troubleshooting: app is missing
chunks.section: Public Edition troubleshooting: app is missing
chunks.content: Do not use PFCG, SU53, STAUTHTRACE, SICF, or Gateway transactions in Public Edition. Source checked 2026-10-15 against SAP Help Portal, SAP Fiori Launchpad for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2608: App Finder and Spaces and Pages.

chunks.heading: Public Edition troubleshooting: app is missing
chunks.section: Public Edition troubleshooting: app is missing
chunks.content:
If the app opens but a request fails with an authorization error, reproduce the issue and inspect Display Authorization Trace for the affected business user. Correct only the failed authorization or restriction evidence shown there; a missing-tile symptom should not be routed to this trace. If the app or required catalog is not available in the tenant's delivered content, confirm the tenant release and app availability, then escalate with the app ID, user, role, timestamp, and reproduction details instead of attempting backend service activation.

Sources checked 2026-10-14: SAP Help, Maintain Business Roles (2608), IAM Information System (2608), Details View for Spaces (2608), Step by Step: Create a New Space and Page for a Business Role (2608), and IAM Administration Apps Reference Table (2602).

chunks.heading: Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy
chunks.section: Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy
chunks.content: ## Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy

chunks.heading: Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy
chunks.section: Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy
chunks.content: For a custom SAP Fiori app in S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2608, configure the RAP service by defining its CDS model in ADT, exposing it with a service definition and OData service binding, and defining the UI with `@UI` annotations. This on-stack developer-extensibility path requires a three-system landscape; where that prerequisite or use case does not fit, choose a supported key-user or side-by-side BTP extension for the app. Create the Fiori elements app with SAP Business Application Studio and SAP Fiori tools. Use BAS's supported deployment task to deploy the UI to the SAPUI5 ABAP Repository; create the IAM app, launchpad target mapping, and business catalog. Assign the catalog and space in Maintain Business Roles, then assign the business role to the user in Maintain Business Users; protect reads with CDS DCL and enforce business actions with application checks. Validate service binding preview, deployed app launch, role assignment, and user-context access.

chunks.heading: Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy
chunks.section: Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy
chunks.content: Do not use PFCG, SEGW, `/IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE`, SU53, or STAUTHTRACE as the Public Edition procedure.

chunks.heading: Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy
chunks.section: Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy
chunks.content: For an ABAP Cloud/RAP service, model the business data in CDS in ABAP Development Tools (ADT), define the service in a service definition, expose it with an OData service binding, and use `@UI` annotations for Fiori elements. Test the service in the service-binding editor and use Fiori elements preview before building the UI. SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2608 documents this service-definition/service-binding path; do not assume `@OData.publish: true` or `SEGW` is the right path for a new RAP service. For an existing OData V2 service in a customer-managed Gateway deployment, check registration/activation in `/IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE`; that transaction does not diagnose runtime errors. OData V4 is managed as a service group; use the service binding and Gateway V4 administration tools supported by that release. The V4 authorization check is `S_START` for `G4BA` service-group objects, not the OData V2 `S_SERVICE` rule.

chunks.heading: Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy
chunks.section: Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy
chunks.content: Build or adapt the SAPUI5/Fiori elements UI with SAP Business Application Studio and SAP Fiori tools, using the system destination and service selected for the project. Choose a deployment supported by the target architecture: the SAPUI5 ABAP Repository for an ABAP-hosted app, or the HTML5 Application Repository on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry for a side-by-side app. BAS generates the deployment configuration and `npm run deploy` uses the configured deployment task; do not prescribe `SE80` or direct BSP editing as the standard current workflow. For S/4HANA Public Edition extensibility, follow the tenant's released ABAP Cloud and deployment path rather than assuming private-system administration access.

chunks.heading: Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy
chunks.section: Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy
chunks.content: Keep launchpad visibility separate from runtime authorization. In Public Edition, publish the supported IAM app and business catalog, assign the catalog and space/page through the business role, and assign that role to the business user. In Private Edition/on-premise, maintain the app descriptor/target mapping and business catalog in the launchpad content tools, then assign the catalog/space and authorizations through PFCG. The exact runtime service authorization depends on OData version and deployment: V2 uses the applicable `IWSG`/`IWSV` and `S_SERVICE` service defaults; V4 uses service-group object `G4BA` with `S_START`. CDS DCL filters authorized read data; write operations and business actions also need their application-specific authorization checks. Name a specific business authorization object only when the service implementation or trace confirms it.

chunks.heading: Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy
chunks.section: Custom Fiori app: design, build, secure, and deploy
chunks.content: Validate each boundary independently: service binding preview and metadata/response; app preview and deployed app launch; target mapping/launchpad content; assigned business role; then a user-context test for both permitted and denied data/actions. For a Public Edition authorization failure use Display Authorization Trace. For ABAP Gateway use the matching hub/backend error log first and trace the authorization check only when the log indicates that layer. `/IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE`, SICF, `/IWFND/V4_ADMIN`, PFCG, and ABAP traces apply only to the relevant customer-managed ABAP deployment and release. A missing tile, a failed OData request, and an unauthorized business operation are distinct failure points.

chunks.heading: SAP Fiori Launchpad Access
chunks.content: # SAP Fiori Launchpad Access

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.content:
## Overview

The SAP Fiori launchpad resolves which apps a user can see from role-assigned catalogs, spaces, and pages, then the backend or cloud authorization model decides what those apps may execute. A missing tile and an opened app that fails are different problems. Source checked 2026-10-21 against knowledge/fiori/fiori-security.md.

chunks.heading: Interview Summary
chunks.content: I would separate launchpad visibility from runtime authorization and keep the tool path with the edition.

chunks.heading: Troubleshoot launchpad visibility before runtime authorization
chunks.section: Troubleshoot launchpad visibility before runtime authorization
chunks.content: I would ask whether the user cannot see the app or whether the app opens and then fails. For a missing app I would stay on launchpad resolution: Public Edition Maintain Business Users, Maintain Business Roles, and Manage Launchpad Spaces; Private Edition or on-premise PFCG role, catalog, target mapping, and /UI2/FLPCM_CUST or /UI2/FLPCM_CONF. I would use Display Authorization Trace on Public Edition, or SU53 and Gateway logs on an ABAP system, only after the app opens and the evidence points to an authorization or service failure. I would validate by having the affected user find the app and complete the intended business task.

chunks.heading: Fiori Spaces and Pages
chunks.content: # Fiori Spaces and Pages

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.content:
## Overview

Spaces and pages control launchpad layout. They do not grant backend authorization by themselves. On Public Edition, spaces and pages are assigned from the business role. On Private Edition and newer on-premise releases (S/4HANA 2020+), spaces and pages are maintained in Manage Launchpad Spaces (Fiori app F2786) and Manage Launchpad Pages (Fiori app F2570) and assigned to a PFCG role; classic Groups are the legacy layout path, not the default current design. Launchpad content for catalogs and target mappings is maintained in /UI2/FLPCM_CUST (client) / /UI2/FLPCM_CONF (cross-client) with App Manager /UI2/FLPAM for technical catalogs where the release supports it. Older on-premise releases may still use groups. Source checked 2026-10-21 against knowledge/fiori/fiori-security.md, SAP Learning Managing Spaces and Pages, and SAP Note 3401525 title and public FAQ text; app IDs F2786/F2570 confirmed against SAP Fiori Apps Reference Library naming for Manage Launchpad Spaces / Pages.

chunks.heading: Interview Summary
chunks.content: I would check space and page assignment when the catalog is present but the app is still missing from the expected page.

chunks.heading: Configure Fiori launchpad spaces and pages on S/4HANA
chunks.section: Configure Fiori launchpad spaces and pages on S/4HANA
chunks.content: ## Configure Fiori launchpad spaces and pages on S/4HANA

chunks.heading: Configure Fiori launchpad spaces and pages on S/4HANA
chunks.section: Configure Fiori launchpad spaces and pages on S/4HANA
chunks.content: To configure the Fiori launchpad layout on S/4HANA 2020+, I default to Spaces and Pages rather than classic Groups. On Private Edition or on-premise I maintain catalogs and target mappings in /UI2/FLPCM_CUST (client) or /UI2/FLPCM_CONF (cross-client), use /UI2/FLPAM for technical catalogs where the release supports it, then maintain layout in Manage Launchpad Spaces (F2786) and Manage Launchpad Pages (F2570) and assign the space on the PFCG business role. OData V2 services are activated in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE; OData V4 uses /IWFND/V4_ADMIN and service-group publishing — I never treat the V2 transaction as universal. Backend runtime still needs S_SERVICE / business-object authorization. On Public Edition I stay in Maintain Business Roles, Manage Launchpad Spaces, and Manage Launchpad Pages without PFCG or /UI2/FLPCM_CUST.

chunks.heading: Configure Fiori launchpad spaces and pages on S/4HANA
chunks.section: Configure Fiori launchpad spaces and pages on S/4HANA
chunks.content: I validate by signing on as the assigned user, confirming the app on the intended page, completing the business action, and using Display Authorization Trace or SU53 / Gateway logs only after the app opens and fails.

chunks.heading: Verify space and page assignment for a missing app
chunks.section: Verify space and page assignment for a missing app
chunks.content: I would confirm whether the app is absent from the whole launchpad or only from the expected page. If App Finder or All My Apps shows the app but the page does not, I would inspect the role's space and page content. On Public Edition that work stays in Maintain Business Roles, Manage Launchpad Spaces, and Manage Launchpad Pages. On Private Edition or on-premise I would confirm the PFCG role assignment of the space after the catalog and target mapping are correct. Spaces and pages do not replace runtime authorization. I would validate by signing on as the affected user and confirming the app appears in the intended space for the business task.

chunks.heading: Access Risk Analysis (ARA)
chunks.content: # Access Risk Analysis (ARA)

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.content:
## Overview

Access Risk Analysis is the GRC component that evaluates segregation of duties conflicts. It runs against a maintained ruleset, checking both existing role assignments and simulated requests before approval, and produces the risk data that drives mitigation decisions and approval routing elsewhere in GRC.

chunks.heading: Interview Summary
chunks.content: ARA compares a user's actual or proposed access against a ruleset defining which combinations of functions create segregation of duties risk. It supports both user-level analysis of existing access and simulation of a new request before it's approved, and its output feeds directly into ARM's approval workflow when a conflict needs risk owner review.

chunks.heading: 30 Second Interview Answer
chunks.content: ARA is the segregation of duties engine in GRC. It compares a user's access, or a proposed request, against a ruleset that defines risky combinations of functions — like someone who can both create a vendor and approve a payment to that vendor. If a conflict is found, that result feeds into the approval workflow, usually requiring a risk owner to review and either approve with a mitigating control or reject the request.

chunks.heading: 60 Second Interview Answer
chunks.content:
ARA, Access Risk Analysis, checks whether a user's access — existing or proposed — creates a segregation of duties conflict. It works against a ruleset, which is a maintained set of rules defining risky combinations, classically things like the ability to both create a vendor master record and post a payment to that vendor.

ARA runs in two main modes. User-level analysis looks at existing access across the organization, which is what periodic access reviews and audits typically use. Simulation runs during a new access request in ARM, checking what would happen if the request were approved, before it actually is. That's what lets GRC flag a conflict at the point of request instead of discovering it during the next audit cycle.

The output of a conflict isn't automatically a rejection — it's a data point that usually routes the request to a risk owner, who decides whether to approve with a documented mitigating control or reject the request and adjust scope instead.

chunks.heading: 90 Second Interview Answer
chunks.content: Access Risk Analysis is the segregation of duties engine underneath GRC Access Control. Its core job is comparing a user's access — either what they already have, or what they're requesting — against a ruleset that defines combinations of functions considered risky when held by the same person. The textbook example is a user who can both create a vendor master record and post a payment, which creates the opportunity for fraud that segregation of duties is designed to prevent.

chunks.heading: 90 Second Interview Answer
chunks.content: ARA operates in two distinct modes that matter for different purposes. User-level analysis evaluates existing access across the user population, which is the mode used for periodic access reviews, audit preparation, and ongoing compliance monitoring — it answers "who currently has a conflict." Simulation mode runs during the ARM request process itself, evaluating what a user's access would look like if a pending request were approved, before it actually is — it answers "would approving this create a conflict." That distinction matters because it's the difference between catching a risk proactively at the point of request versus discovering it after the fact during an audit.

chunks.heading: 90 Second Interview Answer
chunks.content:
When ARA identifies a conflict, that's not automatically a rejection — it's a risk signal that typically routes into the approval workflow, most commonly triggering an additional MSMP stage requiring a risk owner to review the specific conflict. The risk owner then makes a documented decision: approve with a mitigating control that compensates for the risk through a different means, like a compensating review process, or reject the request and push back on scope.

The part that determines whether ARA actually catches real risk is ruleset quality. A ruleset built once and never updated will miss new conflicts as business processes evolve, and it'll keep flagging conflicts that no longer reflect how the business actually operates. Ruleset maintenance is a continuous responsibility, not a one-time configuration task, and it's usually the difference between ARA being a genuinely effective control versus generating noise that risk owners start rubber-stamping through.

chunks.heading: Architecture
chunks.content:
## Architecture

- Ruleset: the maintained definition of risky function combinations
- Function: a business activity, like "create vendor" or "post payment," that rules are built from
- Risk: a defined combination of two or more functions considered conflicting
- User-level analysis: evaluates existing access across the organization
- Simulation: evaluates a proposed request before approval
- Mitigation: a documented compensating control applied when a conflict can't be avoided

chunks.heading: Critical Actions, Critical Permissions, and SoD Risks
chunks.section: Critical Actions, Critical Permissions, and SoD Risks
chunks.content: ARA rulesets distinguish segregation-of-duties Risks from Critical Access Risks.

chunks.heading: Critical Actions, Critical Permissions, and SoD Risks
chunks.section: Critical Actions, Critical Permissions, and SoD Risks
chunks.content:
- A segregation-of-duties Risk requires conflicting Functions held together (for example create vendor plus post payment).
- A Critical Action Risk flags a single sensitive executable on its own — typically a transaction, Web Dynpro application, Fiori UI5 application, or service that is privileged even without a second conflicting Function. In ABAP landscapes the Action layer often aligns to executables checked via `S_TCODE` or equivalent service identifiers, while the Permission layer still carries the authorization-object, field and value combinations that make that Action powerful.
- A Critical Permission Risk flags a sensitive authorization-object, field and value combination on its own, even when the associated Action looks ordinary.
- Critical Action and Critical Permission are therefore single-sided sensitive-access detections. They are not an S/4HANA role-transformation methodology and they are not interchangeable with classic two-function SoD Risks.

chunks.heading: Critical Actions, Critical Permissions, and SoD Risks
chunks.section: Critical Actions, Critical Permissions, and SoD Risks
chunks.content: - Functions, Actions and Permissions still define what ARA evaluates; the difference is whether the Risk needs a conflicting pair or a single powerful Action/Permission. Legitimate Critical Action explanations that name ARA, ruleset tables, Actions, and `S_TCODE`/auth-object combinations must be preserved — they are not generic filler and must not be stripped or replaced by an unrelated S/4 transformation blueprint.

chunks.heading: Runtime Flow
chunks.content:
## Runtime Flow

For user-level analysis, ARA evaluates each user's current role assignments against every rule in the ruleset, flagging any combination of functions the user has access to that matches a defined risk. For simulation, ARA takes the requested access from an in-flight ARM request, combines it conceptually with the user's existing access, and evaluates that combined set against the ruleset before the request is approved. Flagged conflicts are attached to the request or the user's risk profile, and in the ARM context, typically trigger an additional approval stage for risk owner review.

chunks.heading: Configuration
chunks.content:
- Maintain the ruleset to reflect actual business processes and organizational risk tolerance
- Define functions mapping to the authorization objects and values that represent each business activity
- Configure risk levels or categories to prioritize which conflicts require the most scrutiny
- Integrate simulation into the ARM request flow so conflicts are caught before approval, not after

chunks.heading: Implementation Activities
chunks.content:
- Design the ruleset based on the organization's actual business processes and risk appetite
- Map functions to the specific authorization objects and values that represent them
- Run baseline user-level analysis to understand existing conflict exposure before go-live
- Integrate simulation into the access request process

chunks.heading: Migration Activities
chunks.content:
- Validate ruleset accuracy against the migrated or upgraded system's authorization objects
- Re-run baseline analysis after a migration to catch any newly introduced conflicts
- Confirm function definitions still map correctly to authorization data in the target system

chunks.heading: Rollout Activities
chunks.content:
- Extend the ruleset to cover new business processes introduced by the rollout entity
- Run baseline analysis for the new user population before go-live
- Validate that simulation correctly evaluates requests for the new business unit

chunks.heading: Production Support Activities
chunks.content:
- Support risk owners reviewing flagged conflicts during the request process
- Maintain and update the ruleset as business processes change
- Run periodic user-level analysis for ongoing compliance monitoring and audit preparation

chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.content:
Common issue: ARA isn't flagging a conflict that should exist.
Root cause: the ruleset doesn't have a rule covering that specific combination of functions, or the function definitions don't map to the correct authorization objects.
Resolution: review and update the ruleset and function definitions to accurately reflect the risk.

Common issue: ARA is flagging conflicts that don't reflect actual business risk.
Root cause: the ruleset is outdated or overly broad relative to current business processes.
Resolution: review and refine the ruleset with input from business process owners.

Common issue: simulation during a request doesn't match the result of a subsequent user-level analysis for the same user.
Root cause: simulation and user-level analysis may be evaluating against slightly different data timing or scope.
Resolution: review the analysis scope and timing configuration for consistency between the two modes.
